extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of classical Roman history; writers studying historical narrative, leadership, and governance
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the qualities, practices, and judgment calls Tacitus attributes to effective provincial governance and military command (as exemplified in Agricola). Useful for analyzing leadership rhetoric in classical historical narrative or for modeling historical-character behavior in creative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity, temperance, and cleanness of hands
rubrics_metrics.description: "his just dealings, his temperance, and the cleanness of his hands."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tacitus presents integrity and personal temperance as core virtues of good governance; these qualities coexist with authority and are praised as foundational rather than ostentatious. (Surrounding text: his complaisance neither weakened his authority, nor did his severity make him less amiable.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ostentation in pursuit of glory
rubrics_metrics.description: "glory itself was what he pursued, not by any ostentation of bravery, nor by any strain of artifice or address"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue honour quietly and genuinely rather than through showy acts or political artifice; modesty in reputation-building enlarges true fame (Tacitus notes Agricola 'disguising his fame' enlarged it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthfulness and evidence-based historical reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: "will by me be recounted according to the truth of evidence and discoveries."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly frames the account as aiming for accuracy rather than rhetorical embellishment — a criterion for historical writing: rely on evidence and discoveries, avoid inventing picturesque details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the temper and customs of the governed
rubrics_metrics.description: "as he was acquainted with the temper of the people in his Province; as he had also learned from the conduct and experience of others"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective policy and military strategy require understanding local character and institutions; reforms that ignore local temper are less likely to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove causes of unrest beginning at home
rubrics_metrics.description: "he determined to cut off all the causes of war. Beginning therefore with himself and those appertaining to him, he checked and regulated his own household"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To secure peace, reform one's own household and immediate circle first; public example and internal discipline are prerequisites for wider order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep household affairs separate from public business
rubrics_metrics.description: "By none of his domestics, bond or freed, was aught that concerned the public transacted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent corruption and improper influence by ensuring family/household retain no role in official public transactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meritocratic promotion and appointments
rubrics_metrics.description: "in raising the soldiers to a superior class, he was swayed by no personal interest or partiality ... that the best soldiers were ever the most faithful."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose people for office by ability and proven fidelity rather than favoritism or patronage; this fosters troop loyalty and competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate punishment and measured discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: "All that passed he would know; though all that was amiss he would not punish. Upon small offences he bestowed pardon; for such as were great he exercised proportionable severity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise discernment in discipline: pardon minor faults to preserve morale, punish major transgressions firmly; avoid vindictiveness ("from his anger no spleen remained").

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer candidates who will not transgress
rubrics_metrics.description: "In conferring offices and employments he rather chose men who would not transgress, than such as he must afterwards condemn for transgressing."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting officers, prioritize probity and restraint over brilliance likely to lead to misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable taxation and elimination of private exactions
rubrics_metrics.description: "he softened it by causing a just and equal distribution of all public burdens; since he abolished whatever exactions had been devised for the lucre of particulars"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate unrest by fair distribution of taxes and by removing exploitative middlemen or private extortions that increase popular resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead by example; share danger with troops
rubrics_metrics.description: "marching in person before his army"; "himself in the first ship that landed"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal courage and visible sharing of risk are key to inspiring soldiers and consolidating command; being first into danger increases army morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose encampments and stations with care
rubrics_metrics.description: "He himself always chose the ground for encamping... no place of strength founded by him, was ever taken by violence, or abandoned upon articles or despair."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select defensible, well-situated positions personally; good siting of forts and camps prevents losses and need for surrender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct well-provisioned, durable fortifications
rubrics_metrics.description: "against any long siege they were supplied with provisions for a year."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design garrisons to withstand prolonged siege by providing long-term supplies and robust construction; such forts can hold winter and deny the enemy recovery opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use combined sea-and-land operations and naval presence
rubrics_metrics.description: "his fleet... employed by him as part of his forces... by sea and land the war was urged."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate naval power with land forces to deny enemy refuge, intimidate coastal populations, and expand operational reach; a fleet can cause 'consternation and dismay.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ intelligence, scouts, and tactical flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: "having from his spies learnt what route the enemy had taken... commanded the lightest of his foot and cavalry to charge them, whilst yet engaged, in the rear"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reconnaissance to learn enemy movements; employ flexible troop movements (light infantry, cavalry) to strike exposed flanks/rears and turn the tide of engagements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harass then offer peace — combine pressure with leniency
rubrics_metrics.description: "to the enemies all the while allowed not a moment's quiet or recess, but was ever distressing them with sudden incursions and ravages. Then, having sufficiently alarmed and terrified them, his next course was to spare them, thus to tempt them with the sweetness and allurements of peace."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strategy of sustained pressure followed by conciliatory measures can induce submission and reduce future resistance; use military pressure to bring foes to negotiate on favorable terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming others' glory; practice modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: "Nor did Agricola ever arrogate to himself the glory of exploits performed by others... he would not bestow the title of an expedition or of victory... nor with the bare honour of the laurel distinguish these his exploits."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modesty and restraint in claiming honors prevent envy and build broader respect; downplaying one's achievements can paradoxically enlarge reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage cultural and civic assimilation through material incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: "he first privately exhorted them, then publicly assisted them, to build temples, houses and places of assembling... he was already taking care to have the sons of their chiefs taught the liberal sciences"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reconcile conquered peoples by promoting infrastructure, education for elites, and culturally attractive institutions (temples, assemblies, dress), thereby drawing them into the imperial order by incentives rather than sheer coercion.
